practice_bank.title: Practice — The Speed of Light
practice_bank.intro: Eight questions on how fast light travels and how that was first measured.

sections.title: Speed of Light in Different Media
sections.blurb: Only vacuum gives every colour the same speed.

items.prompt: Light passes through a closed cylindrical tube containing a gas. As the gas is gradually pumped out, the speed of light inside the tube will
options: decrease
remain constant
increase
first increase then decrease
items.explanation: The gas has a refractive index slightly above 1, so light travels at $ c/n $, marginally below $ c $. Removing the gas drives $ n $ towards exactly 1, so the speed rises towards $ c $. The change is tiny — air's index is about $ 1.0003 $ — but the direction is unambiguous.

items.prompt: The speeds of red light and yellow light are exactly equal
options: in vacuum but not in air
in air but not in vacuum
in vacuum as well as in air
in neither
items.explanation: In vacuum every wavelength travels at exactly $ c $ — vacuum is non-dispersive. Air, like any material, has a refractive index that varies slightly with wavelength, so the two colours travel at very slightly different speeds. That difference is precisely what makes dispersion possible.

items.prompt: An object in front of a converging lens forms a real image. If the object is shifted slightly,
options: the image shifts a little later
the image shifts at the same instant
the image shifts a little earlier
the image does not shift
items.explanation: Information cannot travel faster than light, so the news of the object's move takes a finite time to reach the lens and then the image plane. The delay is around $ 10^{-9} $ s for laboratory distances — utterly unobservable, but not zero. Strict simultaneity would require infinite signal speed.

items.prompt: The speed of light in a medium of refractive index $ 1.5 $ is
items.explanation: From $ n = c/v $, the speed is $ v = c/n = (3 \times 10^{8})/1.5 = 2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $. Note the speed is always *less* than $ c $ in a material — any answer exceeding $ 3 \times 10^{8} $ should be rejected on sight.

sections.title: Measuring the Speed of Light
sections.blurb: From Roemer's moons to a defined constant.

items.prompt: In Fizeau's toothed-wheel method, light returns through a gap in the wheel when the wheel has rotated by
options: half a tooth spacing
one full revolution
a quarter of a revolution
one full tooth-plus-gap spacing
items.explanation: Light leaves through one gap, travels to a distant mirror and back. For it to pass again, the wheel must have advanced by exactly one tooth-and-gap period so that the *next* gap occupies the same place. Advancing by half that spacing would put a tooth there and block the light — which is how Fizeau found the first blocking speed.

items.prompt: Michelson's rotating-mirror method improved on Fizeau's chiefly because
options: it used a much longer light path than Fizeau had
the returning image is displaced continuously rather than merely blocked
it needed no distant mirror at all, only a rotating one
it worked without any rotating component whatsoever
items.explanation: Fizeau had to judge when the returning light was *extinguished*, which is an imprecise thing to see. A rotating mirror shifts the returning beam through a measurable angle instead, and an angle can be read far more accurately than a fading brightness. That change of observable is what raised the precision.

items.prompt: In the SI system today, the speed of light in vacuum is
options: a measured quantity with an experimental uncertainty
known only to three significant figures
a defined exact constant
different for different observers
items.explanation: Since 1983 the metre has been *defined* as the distance light travels in $ 1/299\,792\,458 $ of a second, which makes $ c $ exact by definition. Improved experiments now refine the metre rather than $ c $. And its constancy for all observers is the founding postulate of special relativity.

items.prompt: Roemer's determination of the speed of light was based on
options: the aberration of starlight over the course of a year
timing eclipses of Jupiter’s moons at different earth-Jupiter distances
a toothed wheel and a mirror several kilometres away
interference between two beams of light from one source
items.explanation: Roemer noticed that eclipses of Io ran late when the earth was far from Jupiter and early when close — the discrepancy being the extra travel time across the earth's orbit. It was the first evidence that light travels at a finite speed at all, obtained astronomically long before any laboratory method existed.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — Speed of light and refractive index
worked_examples.problem: Light travels at $ 2.25 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $ in water. Find water's refractive index, and the time light takes to cross $ 3 $ m of water.
worked_examples.solution:
**Refractive index:**

$ n = \frac{c}{v} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2.25 \times 10^{8}} = 1.33 $

which is the familiar $ 4/3 $.

**Time to cross:**

$ t = \frac{d}{v} = \frac{3}{2.25 \times 10^{8}} = 1.33 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{s} $

about $ 13 $ nanoseconds.

**Compare with vacuum:** the same $ 3 $ m would take $ 10 $ ns. The extra $ 3 $ ns is what the refractive index amounts to physically — a delay.

**A useful way to see optical path.** Light takes as long to cross $ 3 $ m of water as it would to cross $ 4 $ m of vacuum. That equivalent vacuum distance, $ nd $, is the *optical path* — the quantity that governs every interference calculation.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Fizeau's toothed wheel
worked_examples.problem: In a Fizeau experiment the mirror is $ 8.6 $ km away and the wheel has $ 720 $ teeth. Light is first blocked when the wheel spins at $ 12.6 $ revolutions per second. Find the speed of light.
worked_examples.solution:
**The round-trip distance:**

$ 2L = 2(8600) = 17\,200\ \text{m} $

**The time available.** Light is first blocked when the wheel has turned by *half* a tooth-and-gap spacing, so a tooth has moved into the gap's place. With $ 720 $ teeth there are $ 720 $ gaps, so half a spacing is $ \frac{1}{2 \times 720} $ of a revolution.

At $ 12.6 $ rev/s, one revolution takes $ 1/12.6 $ s, so

$ t = \frac{1}{2 \times 720 \times 12.6} = \frac{1}{18\,144} = 5.51 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{s} $

**Speed of light:**

$ c = \frac{2L}{t} = \frac{17\,200}{5.51 \times 10^{-5}} = 3.12 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

Within about 4% of the true value — remarkable for 1849.

**Why the baseline had to be kilometres long.** With $ L $ only a few metres, $ t $ would be nanoseconds and no mechanical wheel could spin fast enough. Choosing a distant mirror is what brings the timing into mechanical reach.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Michelson's rotating mirror
worked_examples.problem: An octagonal mirror rotates so that light returning from a mirror $ 35 $ km away finds the next face exactly in position. Find the rotation rate needed, and hence how the speed of light follows.
worked_examples.solution:
**Round-trip time**, assuming $ c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $:

$ t = \frac{2L}{c} = \frac{2(35\,000)}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 2.33 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{s} $

**Rotation required.** An octagon has 8 faces, so the next face arrives after one eighth of a revolution. That eighth must take $ t $:

$ T = 8t = 1.87 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s} $

$ f = \frac{1}{T} = 536\ \text{rev s}^{-1} $

**How the measurement runs in practice.** The rate is measured with a stroboscope or tuning fork, the distance surveyed, and then

$ c = \frac{2L}{t} = 2L \times 8f = 16 L f $

**Why this design is precise.** Only two quantities enter — a surveyed distance and a rotation rate — and both can be measured to high accuracy. Michelson eventually reached about one part in $ 10^{5} $ this way, and the method held the record for decades.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Roemer's astronomical method
worked_examples.problem: Eclipses of a moon of Jupiter are observed to run about $ 1000 $ s late when the earth is on the far side of its orbit compared with the near side. The earth's orbital diameter is $ 3.0 \times 10^{11} $ m. Estimate the speed of light.
worked_examples.solution:
The delay is simply the extra time light needs to cross the earth's orbit.

$ c = \frac{\text{extra distance}}{\text{extra time}} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{11}}{1000} = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Why this was such a leap.** Before Roemer, light was widely assumed to travel instantaneously. His observation showed the eclipses were systematically early or late in step with the earth-Jupiter distance — a pattern only a finite light speed could explain.

**The clever part of the method.** Jupiter's moons are a *clock* of known period. Any drift in the observed timing must therefore come from the changing travel distance, not from the moons. Roemer needed no precision timing apparatus at all — only patience and a predictable astronomical event.

**Where the error lay.** The main uncertainty was the size of the earth's orbit, which was poorly known in 1676. His speed was about 26% low, but the *method* was sound, and it remained the only approach for nearly two centuries.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — Light-travel times across astronomical distances
worked_examples.problem: Find the time light takes to reach the earth from (a) the moon, $ 3.84 \times 10^{8} $ m away, (b) the sun, $ 1.5 \times 10^{11} $ m away. Express the second as a light-time.
worked_examples.solution:
**(a) From the moon:**

$ t = \frac{3.84 \times 10^{8}}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 1.28\ \text{s} $

**(b) From the sun:**

$ t = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{11}}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 500\ \text{s} = 8.3\ \text{minutes} $

**What this means physically.** You never see the sun as it is now, only as it was eight minutes ago. The round-trip delay to the moon — about $ 2.6 $ s — is audible in radio conversations with lunar missions and is exactly why those exchanges sound stilted.

**The light-year as a distance.** A year has $ 3.15 \times 10^{7} $ s, so

$ 1\ \text{light-year} = (3 \times 10^{8})(3.15 \times 10^{7}) = 9.5 \times 10^{15}\ \text{m} $

The nearest star is $ 4.2 $ light-years off, so its light left before you read this sentence by more than four years. Looking outward in space is always looking backward in time.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Delay introduced by a slab
worked_examples.problem: A glass slab of thickness $ 6 $ cm and refractive index $ 1.5 $ is placed in a light beam. By how much is the light delayed compared with travelling the same $ 6 $ cm through vacuum?
worked_examples.solution:
**Time through the glass:**

$ v = \frac{c}{n} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

$ t_{glass} = \frac{0.06}{2 \times 10^{8}} = 3.0 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{s} $

**Time through the same distance of vacuum:**

$ t_{vac} = \frac{0.06}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{s} $

**Delay:**

$ \Delta t = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{s} = 100\ \text{ps} $

**Express it as extra optical path:**

$ \Delta t \times c = (1.0 \times 10^{-10})(3 \times 10^{8}) = 0.03\ \text{m} = 3\ \text{cm} $

which is exactly $ (n-1)t = (0.5)(6) = 3 $ cm — the extra optical path met in the interference chapter.

**The connection worth seeing.** A time delay and an extra optical path are the same fact in two currencies. In interference we count that extra path in wavelengths; here we count it in picoseconds. Both describe the light simply arriving late.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Light-travel time and satellite navigation
worked_examples.problem: A navigation satellite is $ 20\,000 $ km from a receiver. Find the signal travel time, and the position error that a timing error of $ 1 $ nanosecond would cause.
worked_examples.solution:
**Travel time:**

$ t = \frac{d}{c} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{7}}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 0.067\ \text{s} = 67\ \text{ms} $

**Position error from a $ 1 $ ns timing error:**

$ \Delta d = c\,\Delta t = (3 \times 10^{8})(10^{-9}) = 0.3\ \text{m} $

Thirty centimetres per nanosecond.

**Why this sets the whole engineering problem.** Satellite navigation works by measuring travel times from several satellites and solving for position. Since every nanosecond costs $ 30 $ cm, metre-level accuracy demands clocks good to a few nanoseconds over the whole constellation — hence atomic clocks aboard every satellite.

**And why relativity is not optional here.** A satellite clock runs fast relative to a ground clock by about $ 38 $ microseconds a day, once gravitational and motional effects are combined. Left uncorrected that is $ 38\,000 $ ns, or roughly $ 11 $ km of position error accumulating daily. Navigation systems correct for it explicitly — one of the most routine practical uses of relativity there is.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — Aberration of starlight
worked_examples.problem: The earth orbits the sun at $ 30\ \text{km s}^{-1} $. Find the angle by which the apparent direction of a star overhead is shifted, and explain how this yields the speed of light.
worked_examples.solution:
**The shift.** The earth's motion tilts the apparent direction of incoming starlight, much as a moving cyclist must tilt an umbrella. For a star perpendicular to the earth's motion,

$ \tan\theta = \frac{v}{c} = \frac{3 \times 10^{4}}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 10^{-4} $

$ \theta \approx 10^{-4}\ \text{rad} = 20.6\ \text{arcseconds} $

**What an observer sees.** Over a year the earth's velocity swings right round, so every star traces a small ellipse on the sky with a semi-major axis of about $ 20.5 $ arcseconds — the constant of aberration. Bradley discovered this in 1728.

**How it gives $ c $.** Measure the aberration angle and know the earth's orbital speed, and $ c = v/\tan\theta $ follows directly. Bradley obtained a value within a few per cent of the modern one — more than a century before any laboratory method existed.

**Why aberration is not parallax.** Parallax depends on the earth's *position* and so on the star's distance; aberration depends on the earth's *velocity* and is the same for every star. Distinguishing the two was itself a significant achievement, and it is the reason Bradley found $ c $ while looking for something else entirely.
